problem.title: Large-scale document classification
problem.context: An insurer receives between two and eight million documents a day (scanned forms, e-mails, PDFs) and classifies each one into one of 60 claim types with an LLM-based classifier. Volume varies strongly over the year: storm season brings four times the usual load. Three teams use the results: claims handling, fraud investigation and analytics. The documents contain personal data.

requirements.text: Classify every incoming document into a claim type, with a confidence.
Deliver the results to the three consuming teams.
Send the documents the classifier is unsure about to human review, and use the reviewers' corrections to improve the classifier.
During storm season, at eight million documents a day, every document is classified within two hours of arrival.
When classification quality drops for one claim type (for example, after a form changes its layout), operators see it within one day.
The classification costs less than 0.2 cents per document on average over the year.
A consuming team can change how it processes the results without the other teams or the classifier having to change.
The documents contain personal data and may not leave the EU.
The classifier uses an LLM from the insurer's approved provider, in its EU region.

values: Inference: One approved EU LLM call per document
Scheduling: Durable asynchronous queue with autoscaling workers
Delivery: Publish versioned results to shared event stream
Human feedback: Confidence threshold routes uncertain cases to reviewers; corrections feed periodic training
Monitoring: Daily per-claim-type quality and drift dashboard
points.description: Each document is processed by one approved EU LLM call through a durable asynchronous queue, with autoscaling workers publishing versioned results to a shared event stream. Low-confidence cases go to reviewers, whose corrections inform periodic training, while a daily dashboard tracks quality and drift by claim type. Trade-off: This provides scalable, durable, auditable processing and a feedback loop, but asynchronous handling and periodic training delay improvements, daily monitoring may miss rapid changes, and the single approved model limits inference flexibility.

Trade-off: This gains cost control, scalable processing, traceability, and feedback-driven improvement, but gives up immediacy through asynchronous processing, periodic retraining, and daily rather than real-time monitoring. Reviewer capacity and fallback use can also increase operating costs.

Trade-off: This gains governed, reproducible team consumption, scalable throughput, and targeted quality improvement. It gives up immediate inference responsiveness and incurs provider, scheduling, review, and periodic-feedback overhead.

points.description: The system sends each document to multiple LLM calls in parallel, waits synchronously for their responses, and combines their outputs into a consensus. It returns results directly through APIs to consuming teams, routes disagreements and low-confidence cases to human reviewers, and reports aggregate quality across claim types. Trade-off: This improves confidence, visibility, and targeted review, but increases inference cost and synchronous latency while potentially overwhelming reviewers with all flagged cases.

cons: Teams may need polling or separate change notifications
options.reason: It is viable but less direct for independently changing consumers than event delivery.

options.name: Per-type topics with shared contracts
values: Delivery: Versioned per-type result topics with shared event contracts
pros: Combines type-specific streams with common consumer contracts
cons: Creates more topics and access policies to govern in the EU
options.reason: E1 uses shared contracts to keep per-type publishing from coupling consumers.

adrs.title: Turn review corrections into model improvement
adrs.context: Uncertain classifications must receive human review, and corrections must improve the classifier. The feedback path should support per-type quality diagnosis while keeping review and release costs sustainable.

options.name: Periodic correction training
values: Human feedback: Confidence threshold routes uncertain cases to reviewers; corrections feed periodic training
pros: Collects corrections for a repeatable training cycle
cons: Improvements wait for the next periodic cycle
options.reason: B1 favors a controlled periodic loop while focusing its primary refinement on cost monitoring.

options.name: Daily prompt and model release review
values: Human feedback: Confidence threshold routes uncertain cases to reviewers; corrections feed daily prompt and model release review
pros: Creates a daily, governed path from corrections to improvement
cons: Requires reviewer and release-management capacity
options.reason: A1 and C1 use daily release review to shorten the feedback cycle.

options.name: Update specialist prompts from corrections
values: Human feedback: Confidence threshold routes uncertain cases to reviewers; corrections update versioned specialist prompts
pros: Directs each correction toward the affected claim type
cons: Requires prompt review and version management across types
options.reason: E1 aligns correction ownership with claim-type specialization.

options.name: Review all disagreements
values: Human feedback: All disagreements and low-confidence cases go to reviewers
pros: Captures more possible errors for review
cons: Can overwhelm human review capacity
options.reason: Consensus-driven review volume is costly and was not tied to a sustainable feedback cadence.

options.name: Sampled and uncertain review with daily release review
values: Human feedback: Sampled and uncertain cases go to reviewers; corrections feed daily prompt and model release review
pros: Samples model behavior while prioritizing uncertain documents for review
Creates a daily governed correction path
cons: Sampling and release review require reviewer and operations capacity
options.reason: C1 combines broad sampling with targeted uncertainty review to improve confidence in the batch classifier.

adrs.title: Detect claim-type quality regressions
adrs.context: A layout change can degrade one type while aggregate quality remains stable. Operators need a signal within one day, with enough detail to connect the regression to reviewer corrections and model changes.

options.name: Daily per-type alerting
values: Monitoring: Alerting per-claim-type quality dashboard with daily detection objective
pros: Directly measures the one-day detection goal by claim type
cons: Detection depends on labeled outcomes and sufficient sample volume
options.reason: A1 and C1 target the stated observability window.

options.name: Quality and fallback-rate alerts
values: Monitoring: Near-real-time per-claim-type quality alerts and fallback-rate dashboard
pros: Adds faster type-level signals and a cost-relevant fallback metric
cons: More metrics and alerts require tuning
options.reason: B1 makes cascade economics and quality shifts visible together.

options.name: Quality alerts with correction tracking
values: Monitoring: Near-real-time per-claim-type quality alerts and reviewer-correction tracking
pros: Links quality shifts to correction patterns by type
cons: Requires consistent reviewer labels and many monitored streams
options.reason: E1 uses the specialist structure to make regressions actionable.

options.name: Aggregate quality only
values: Monitoring: Aggregate quality dashboard across all claim types
pros: Simple overall health view
cons: Can conceal a decline limited to one type
options.reason: Aggregate-only quality does not adequately expose the example per-type regression.
